images.caption: Figure 1:Overview of LaLa-World.(a)Language provides a shared interface for numerical actions and visual change, enabling joint training on control and video data.(b)A single predictor built on a language model uses encoded observations and language conditions to predict future visual representations. Fine-tuning the pretrained LaLa-World yields LaLa-Policy, which predicts actions as well as future visual representations.(c)The jointly trained predictor achieves higher average MPC planning performance than both separately trained LWM baselines and the generative world model baseline, RAEv2.(d)LaLa-Policy performs competitively with our adapted Cosmos Policy baseline on RoboCasa, while reducing average inference time per trajectory by a factor of5.5×5.5\times.

Figure 2:MPC planning with language actions.LaLa-World imagines future representations under candidate actions with MPC and selects the most promising action toward the goal.
Because all actions share one language interface, a single LaLa-World predictor can plan across multiple domains, despite differences in action dimensionality and physical meaning.
The predictor also supports language-based actions without numerical values (bottom two rows), as detailed inSectionD.4.3.
The visualized observations result from executing the selected actions in the simulator.

Figure 3:Examples of language-conditioned transition data.Each example consists of past observations, a language condition, and the next observation.
Language conditions describe either numerical control actions from simulation and robotics or visual changes in images and videos.
This shared interface enables training a single LWM across different action spaces and data sources.

Figure 5:Latent vs. generative world models for MPC planning under matched setups.We match the vision encoder, language conditions, and training data to compare the two world models.
(a) We track planning performance over training time for full-depth predictors under a 12-hour training budget.
(b) We compare planning performance and average planning time per trajectory across four predictor depths, with all models trained on the same number of transition data.
These results show that LaLa-World achieves higher planning performance than RAEv2 with lower training cost and planning time.

Figure 6:Visualization of predicted future states during MPC planning on DROID.We visualize decoded predictions from LaLa-World and RAEv2, using one or five denoising steps for RAEv2. Each example shows the initial and goal observations, the predicted rollout under the selected language actions, and planning time. Decoded images from LaLa-World may have lower visual quality because it is not trained for pixel reconstruction.
Both models predict plausible future states, while LaLa-World requires less planning time.

Figure 7:Predicted future observations on LIBERO and RoboCasa.Each example shows the initial observation and task instruction, followed by simulator observations during policy execution (upper row) and decoded future predictions (lower row).
LaLa-Policy predicts(xt,ℓ)→(e^t+N,a^t:t+N−1)(x_{t},\ell)\xrightarrow{}(\hat{e}_{t+N},\hat{a}_{t:t+N-1}), and the simulator executesa^t:t+N−1\hat{a}_{t:t+N-1}to yieldxt+Nx_{t+N}; see Equation3.
Since LaLa-Policy is not trained for pixel reconstruction, decoded images may contain visual inaccuracies.

Figure B:ImageNet training pairs and transformation retrieval.Left: a source image and a transformed view form a training pair, with the transformation described in language.
Right: the predicted representation is used to rank 256 transformed views of the same validation image; a subset is illustrated.
The outlined view is the target specified by the language action.

Figure D:Qualitative Results of Communicable World Modeling with an LLM Actor.Each row shows the initial and goal observations and the simulator observations after executing the lowest-cost sequence written by the LLM, with its language action below each frame.
Below the goal observation, we list the cost of the best sequence at each round, which decreases as the LLM revises its plans from the returned costs.

Figure M:Numerical language actions on Wall.Initial and goal observations bracket decoded future predictions (top) and PCA visualizations of predicted latents (bottom), with the selected language actions below each frame.
Figure N:Numerical language actions on PointMaze.Each row shows initial and goal observations and decoded future predictions under the selected actions, which specify pushing forces and directions.

Figure O:Numerical language actions on Push-T.Initial and goal observations bracket decoded future predictions under the selected pusher movements, with numerical displacements described below each frame.
Figure P:Numerical language actions on MetaWorld.Decoded predictions are shown before and after replanning from the simulator observationxt+3​Δx_{t+3\Delta}, alongside initial and goal observations.
Figure Q:Numerical language actions on DROID.Each row shows an initial observation, three decoded future predictions, and the goal observation, with language actions below.

Figure R:Numerical language actions on RoboCasa Reach.Decoded future predictions under selected gripper actions are shown between initial and goal observations. RoboCasa is excluded from world-model training.
Figure S:Numerical language actions on RoboCasa Place.Initial and goal observations bracket decoded future predictions during object placement, with the selected gripper actions below each frame.
Figure T:Qualitative language actions on Wall.Simulator observations show the agent passing through the opening toward the goal. Actions describe directions and relative movement magnitudes.
Figure U:Qualitative language actions on PointMaze.Simulator observations show the ball moving through the maze under MPC, with pushing directions and qualitative force descriptions below the frames.
Figure V:Qualitative language actions on Push-T.Initial and goal observations bracket simulator states during MPC, with the pusher’s direction and relative displacement described below each frame.

Figure W:Qualitative language actions on MetaWorld.Simulator observations show reaching trajectories planned using descriptions of gripper motion and grip adjustment without exact numerical magnitudes.

Figure X:Qualitative language actions on RoboCasa Reach.Simulator observations show zero-shot MPC execution toward the goal, conditioned on qualitative descriptions of gripper translation, rotation, and opening or closing.
Figure Y:Qualitative language actions on RoboCasa Place.Simulator observations show an object-placement trajectory under MPC, with qualitative gripper actions and the goal observation for reference.

Figure Z:LIBERO Spatial: bowl on a ramekin.LaLa-Policy moves the bowl from the ramekin onto the plate. Primary and wrist views compare simulator observations (upper rows) with decoded future predictions (lower rows).

Figure AA:LIBERO Spatial: bowl next to a cookie box.LaLa-Policy moves the specified bowl onto the plate. Simulator observations and decoded future predictions are paired for the primary and wrist views.
Figure AB:LIBERO Object: alphabet soup.LaLa-Policy picks up the alphabet soup and places it in the basket. Each camera view pairs observed states with decoded future predictions.

Figure AE:LIBERO Goal: bowl inside the drawer.LaLa-Policy opens the top drawer and places the bowl inside. Both camera views pair simulator observations with decoded future predictions.

Figure AG:LIBERO Long: stove and moka pot.LaLa-Policy turns on the stove and places the moka pot on it. Primary and wrist views compare simulator observations with decoded future predictions.

Figure AH:RoboCasa: pressing the coffee-machine button.Simulator observations (upper rows) and decoded future predictions (lower rows) show LaLa-Policy pressing the button, from two external views and the wrist view.
Figure AI:RoboCasa: serving a mug.LaLa-Policy moves the mug from beneath the coffee-machine dispenser to the counter. Each of the three views compares observed states with decoded future predictions.
Figure AJ:RoboCasa: opening a microwave.Simulator observations and decoded future predictions show LaLa-Policy opening the microwave door, from the primary, secondary, and wrist views.

Figure AL:RoboCasa: counter-to-cabinet transfer.LaLa-Policy picks up the bar from the counter and places it in the cabinet. Each camera view compares observed states with decoded future predictions.
